summary:
Sejong stands under the national framework of South Korea. Consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal and gender identity or gender expression is not criminalised in civilian life, but Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment; the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

The punitive edge of that regime is documented. In 2017 the military charged 32 personnel in what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, and a soldier received six months for consensual sex. Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a panel treated the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a handicap; she died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition no longer depends on surgery. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that conditioning a gender change on surgery is contrary to law and that judicial guidelines once treated as criteria are now reference only; the court stated that every person has the right to form their character and live according to their gender identity. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender people with minor children may be legally recognised provided they are unmarried, overturning an eleven-year-old precedent, itself an extension of a 2011 ruling that had required applicants to be over 20, single and childless.

Relationship recognition remains closed. South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt; the 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the principal advance in that area. No comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity. LGBTI organisations can register, but an NGO's registration win at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 drew a government appeal and years of bureaucratic obstruction, as Human Rights Watch described it.

Restroom access is a live legal and institutional problem. A Korea Times report of 22 July 2024 records that the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a claim of 3 million won, holding that police advice telling a person who had obtained family-register approval to change sex in 2020 to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights, and that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found 41% avoiding facilities out of fear. Research presented by the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong on 20 March 2024 shows trans teenagers avoiding school restrooms to avoid being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding in and leaving early.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare refused to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Violence concentrates at public events. At an Incheon Pride event about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, after which organisers filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; Busan's 2018 Pride required some 2,000 police to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt unsafe walking the street in the absence of a nondiscrimination bill.

Discrimination is measured at scale. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates; 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma; a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults facing harsh discrimination in the preceding year. A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes a comparatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.
tangentialFactors:
South Korea's legal position differs sharply between the civilian and military spheres, and the military provisions are enforced rather than dormant: the 2017 charging of 32 personnel and the six-month sentence show a live enforcement pattern that has no civilian equivalent.

The trajectory on gender recognition runs against the direction of the military regime. The 8 May 2024 ruling at Yeongdong and the 24 November 2022 Supreme Court decision removed two long-standing barriers, surgery and parenthood, within two years of each other, and the court's reasoning about outdated guidelines being reference rather than criteria gives trans litigants an argument beyond the specific facts.

Documentation activity is itself a signal of turbulence. Litigation over restroom advice, youth-centre research on school facilities, a National Human Rights Commission finding against a ministry, and a peer-reviewed nationwide survey published in June 2025 all indicate contested terrain where outcomes are being fought over rather than settled.

Conversion-therapy and harassment figures come from studies of LGBTQ people generally rather than transgender respondents specifically, so they describe the surrounding climate for a trans visitor more than a trans-specific rate.

Recognition for transgender parents with minor children is available provided the applicant is unmarried.

No comprehensive anti-discrimination statute protects sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex couples cannot marry, enter a civil union or jointly adopt, which shapes hospital visitation, inheritance and parenting for residents even where the 2024 Constitutional Court healthcare ruling provides a limited exception.

outOfScopeNotes:
No Sejong-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding touching trans people appears in the sources supplied; the record for this jurisdiction is the national position as interpreted by the courts, and whether Sejong Metropolitan Government has issued any local guidance on restroom or hospitalisation access is not sourced here.

The restroom case is dated differently across sources: the parent framework records a Seoul Central District Court ruling final on 2 July 2024, while the Korea Times report of 22 July 2024 describes an appellate court dismissing the state's appeal. Whether these describe successive stages of one action or inconsistent reporting is unresolved.

The reach of the surgery-free recognition holding beyond the five applicants at Yeongdong, and the practical effect of the November 2023 National Human Rights Commission finding on ministry practice, are not documented in the supplied material.

Enforcement of article 92-6 within Sejong, and any military installation near the jurisdiction from which personnel there could be affected, are not sourced.
